Business rule placement

  • Alistair Cockburn describes adapters that let different clients drive the same application behavior. Here the HTTP handler and queue worker each translate a request and call the booking operation. Hexagonal Architecture
  • Martin Fowler describes organizing a business transaction as a procedure. This playbook starts a small use case with a named function. More elaborate domain objects become useful when several operations share behavior. Transaction Script
  • PostgreSQL documents how a primary key enforces uniqueness, how an insert handles a conflict on a chosen key, and how Read Committed gives each statement its own snapshot. The example adopts those database semantics. The lifetime of a claim, the replay identity and the caller responses are decisions specific to the example. Constraints, INSERT and Transaction Isolation.
  • PostgreSQL's pg_blocking_pids identifies sessions blocking another session. The two-session exercise uses it to observe actual contention before allowing the first reservation to commit. Session Information Functions.

Module boundaries and failures

  • Cockburn describes application ports and technology-specific adapters. Here booking owns the operations used by its callers and storage adapter. The application wires a function or interface to a concrete implementation. Hexagonal Architecture
  • AWS describes caller-provided request identifiers for recognizing a retry after a lost response. Here retries carry the original actor, slot and claim ID so the service can recover the stored confirmation. Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
  • RFC 9110 defines HTTP status semantics. The booking example chooses 409 for a competing claim and 503 for a temporary inability to confirm a result. The claim ID and retry policy belong to the application. HTTP Semantics, status codes
  • RabbitMQ describes consumer acknowledgements, redelivery and the cost of immediate requeue loops. Here the worker acknowledges terminal outcomes after recording them and uses bounded retries for transient failures. Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms

Safe refactoring

  • Michael Feathers describes characterization tests as a way to discover and record existing behavior. Here the tests observe the HTTP response, worker acknowledgement and stored reservation before the first edit. Characterization Testing
  • Martin Fowler describes refactoring in small steps that preserve observable behavior. His Extract Function example names a piece of existing logic and replaces it with a call. Here we use that move to share the booking decision and verify each caller as it switches over. Refactoring and Extract Function.
